51.event_title: Abigail Adams runs the family farm and finances during the Revolution
51.event: From early in their marriage Abigail Adams proved exceptionally capable of managing the family's finances and household. When John Adams left for the Continental Congress in Philadelphia in 1774, and later served as a diplomat in Europe from 1778, she stayed on the farm at Braintree, managing it and the family's business affairs, paying the bills, coping with wartime shortages and educating their children. She also made investments, including trading in war bonds and a small business importing European goods, that added to the family's prosperity.
51.explanation: Abigail Adams kept the household not only running but growing through a decade of war and separation, freeing her husband for public service.
51.tie_back: The kural defines the true life-partner as one who has the qualities household life needs and orders it to suit her husband's means, and Abigail Adams managed the Adams farm and finances wisely through years of scarcity.
51._accuracy_note: Closely matches the kural's picture of a capable partner who fits the household to its means, even going beyond it by enlarging those means.

52.event_title: Queen Victoria withdraws from public life after Prince Albert's death
52.place: Windsor, Balmoral and Osborne, United Kingdom
52.event: Prince Albert died in December 1861 at the age of 42. Queen Victoria, who had relied on him as her husband and principal trusted adviser in affairs of state, wore black for the rest of her reign and for years rarely appeared in public, spending long periods at Balmoral and Osborne. The public, at first sympathetic, grew increasingly impatient with its absent sovereign, and only gradually, from the late 1860s and 1870s, did she resume her public duties.
52.explanation: Victoria's long seclusion shows how the loss of a life-partner could empty even the grandest position of its meaning for the one left behind.
52.tie_back: The kural says that without a worthy life-partner a household's splendour amounts to nothing, and Victoria, still ruler of a vast empire, found the throne's splendour hollow once the partner who shared her life was gone.
52._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the roles are reversed (a queen losing her husband rather than a man lacking a worthy wife), and the kural speaks of a partner's character rather than her loss, but it vividly shows splendour made empty without the partner.

53.event_title: Empress Theodora counsels Justinian to stand firm in the Nika revolt
53.event: In January 532 the rival Blue and Green factions of Constantinople united in revolt against Emperor Justinian, burned much of the city centre and proclaimed a rival emperor. Justinian's advisers urged him to flee, but Empress Theodora, his most trusted adviser, counselled him to stay; according to the historian Procopius she told the council that she would rather die an empress than live as a fugitive. Justinian stayed, his generals put down the revolt, and he kept his throne for another thirty-three years.
53.explanation: Theodora's resolve at the decisive moment preserved Justinian's reign, and historians regard her as probably the most powerful woman in Byzantine history.
53.tie_back: The kural asks what a man can lack if his wife is truly excellent, and Justinian, on the point of losing everything, kept his empire because of his wife's steadiness.
53._accuracy_note: A strong dramatisation of the first half of the kural; her exact words come to us only through Procopius.

54.event_title: Maria van Reigersberch frees Hugo Grotius from Loevestein Castle
54.event: The Dutch jurist Hugo Grotius was sentenced to life imprisonment at Loevestein Castle in 1618 after a political and religious crisis. His wife, Maria van Reigersberch, who was allowed to visit, noticed that the guards had stopped inspecting the large chest in which books were regularly delivered to him, and with her maid she arranged for him to hide inside it. On 22 March 1621 the chest was carried out of the castle, Grotius escaped to Antwerp, and Maria stayed behind to keep up the pretence; she was not punished, and the couple were reunited in Paris.
54.explanation: The escape, planned by his wife, freed the man later called the father of international law to continue his life's work.
54.tie_back: The kural asks what greater treasure there could be than a woman of steadfast firmness of mind, and Maria van Reigersberch's calm, loyal resolve saved her husband's liberty.
54._accuracy_note: A strong picture of a wife's firmness and devotion as a priceless treasure, though karpu in the kural refers specifically to fidelity of mind rather than courage or ingenuity.

55.event_title: Kasturba Gandhi prepares to speak in her husband's place
55.event: Kasturba Gandhi often took her husband's place in public campaigns when he was in prison. When Mahatma Gandhi was arrested at the start of the Quit India movement in August 1942, before he could address a planned public meeting at Shivaji Park in Bombay, he wanted Kasturba to speak in his place; she prepared a message for the crowd but was arrested on her way to the meeting. She was later held with her husband at the Aga Khan Palace in Pune, where she died in February 1944.
55.explanation: Kasturba's lifelong devotion to her husband and his cause gave her a voice and standing of her own that crowds respected.
55.tie_back: The kural claims that a wife wholly devoted to her husband commands such power that rain falls at her word, and Kasturba's devotion made her the one chosen to speak with her husband's authority when he could not.
55._accuracy_note: Next-best only: no historical event can show a person commanding the rain, and this couplet's literal claim is contested even among commentators; Kasturba illustrates only the authority that devotion can confer.

56.event_title: Ruth Williams Khama stands by Seretse Khama through exile
56.event: In September 1948 Ruth Williams, the daughter of a retired British army officer, married Seretse Khama, heir to the chieftaincy of the Bangwato people of Bechuanaland. The marriage caused controversy in Britain and Bechuanaland, and under pressure from South Africa's government the British exiled the couple to England in 1951. After five years they were allowed to return home as private citizens in 1956, and Seretse went on to become the first president of independent Botswana in 1966.
56.explanation: The Khamas' marriage withstood official disapproval and years of exile, and their partnership became part of the story of a new nation.
56.tie_back: The kural describes the true wife as one who guards herself, cherishes her husband, keeps the household's good name and never slackens, and Ruth Khama remained steadfast at her husband's side through exile and public hostility.
56._accuracy_note: Shows unwavering constancy and care for her husband, but the sources say little about the other duties the kural lists, such as guarding the household's good name.

57.event_title: Begum Rokeya publishes Sultana's Dream and founds a girls' school
57.event: In 1905 Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain, known as Begum Rokeya, published Sultana's Dream in The Indian Ladies' Magazine of Madras, a satire set in Ladyland, where educated women run the country and it is the men who are kept in seclusion. After her husband's death in 1909 she opened a school for Muslim girls at Bhagalpur in his memory, and on 16 March 1911 she re-established the Sakhawat Memorial Girls' School in Calcutta with eight students. Throughout her life she argued that extreme seclusion kept women backward and helpless and that education was the path to their freedom.
57.explanation: Rokeya became a pioneer of women's education and liberation in Bengal, challenging the assumption that confinement was what kept women virtuous.
57.tie_back: The kural asks what confinement can ever achieve and says the only real guard is a woman's own inner steadiness, and Rokeya's satire and schools argued that education and self-command, not seclusion, are what truly guard women.
57._accuracy_note: Captures the kural's rejection of enforced confinement well, though Rokeya argued for education and freedom rather than for karpu as such.

58.event_title: Clara Schumann carries Robert Schumann's music to the world
58.place: Germany and concert halls across Europe
58.event: After Robert Schumann entered an asylum near Bonn in 1854 and died there in 1856, Clara Schumann, widowed at 37 with seven children, supported the family through decades of concert tours across Europe. She made a mission of sharing her husband's music with audiences, and many of his works had their first performances because of her. In her later years she edited his collected works and in 1886 published an instructive edition of his piano music.
58.explanation: Clara Schumann became one of the most celebrated pianists of the nineteenth century while making her husband's music known and preserved.
58.tie_back: The kural promises great glory to women who honour the husband they have received, and Clara Schumann, devoted to performing and preserving Robert's music, won lasting fame alongside his.
58._accuracy_note: Partial fit: the glory the kural promises is in the world of the celestials, while Clara's fame is earthly and owed as much to her own artistry as to honouring her husband.

59.event_title: Julius Caesar divorces Pompeia after the Bona Dea scandal
59.event: In December 62 BCE the women-only rites of the Bona Dea were held in the house of Julius Caesar, then pontifex maximus, presided over by his wife Pompeia, and the politician Publius Clodius Pulcher was discovered to have entered disguised as a woman. Caesar divorced Pompeia at once, yet when called as a witness at Clodius's trial he said he knew nothing about the charges. According to Plutarch, when the prosecutor asked why, then, he had divorced his wife, Caesar answered that his wife ought not even to be under suspicion.
59.explanation: Caesar's reply became proverbial for the idea that a public figure's standing depends on his household being beyond reproach.
59.tie_back: The kural says a man whose wife does not guard the household's good name cannot hold his head high before his critics, and Caesar, an ambitious public man, ended his marriage rather than let any suspicion touch his household.
59._accuracy_note: Closely tied to the kural's concern for the household's reputation and the husband's public standing, though Pompeia's own wrongdoing was never established.

60.event_title: The Curies: a shared Nobel Prize and a daughter who won her own
60.event: Marie and Pierre Curie, married in 1895, worked side by side on radioactivity, and in 1903 Marie became the first woman to receive a Nobel Prize, sharing the physics prize with Pierre and Henri Becquerel after Pierre insisted that his wife share the honour. Their elder daughter, Irène, became a physical chemist, and in 1935 she and her husband Frédéric Joliot-Curie were jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their discovery of artificially produced radioactive isotopes.
60.explanation: The Curie household produced two generations of Nobel laureates, a record of family achievement unmatched in science.
60.tie_back: The kural calls the wife's excellence the blessing of the home and good children its jewel, and Marie Curie's excellence was crowned by a daughter who followed her to a Nobel Prize.
60._accuracy_note: A fitting image of an excellent wife and a jewel-like child, though the kural's mangalam is a broader domestic blessing than scientific achievement.
